title: Capacity Assurance Storyboard for Technical Procurement
summary: A technical-facing storyboard to help procurement committees evaluate dedicated inference capacity offers. Focuses on measurable SLOs, isolation semantics, throughput economics, and negotiation levers tailored for engineering and infra reviewers.
body:
Purpose:
- Translate product-level guarantees into concrete evaluation criteria for technical procurement committees (SRE, infra architects, legal, finance).
- Provide ready-to-use phrasing, counters to common competitor claims, and a procurement checklist that balances cost predictability with operational flexibility.

Context and audience:
- Audience: platform architects, SRE leads, procurement engineers, and legal security reviewers.
- Use-case: enterprise teams buying reserved GPU capacity for production LLM workloads that require predictable per-request latency and throughput, plus data isolation.

Why this framing matters:
- Procurement committees care about two things: predictable economics (committed throughput/cost) and operational safety (isolation, fallbacks, incident runbooks).
- Sales messages that are vague about isolation or use-case coverage create long procurement cycles. This storyboard aims to reduce back-and-forth by surfacing the exact technical asks and trade-offs up front.

Key definitions to align on (recommended language for contracts/PRDs):
- Guaranteed throughput: tokens/sec per committed GPU expressed as p95 sustained throughput over 24h windows. Example: "Committed throughput: 350k tokens/sec per p4d cluster, measured at customer input distribution, p95 over 24h."
- Latency SLOs: p50/p95/p99 tail latencies for typical prompt sizes with clear test harness (prompt set + attachment of token counts).
- Isolation envelope: description of compute/data isolation (dedicated GPU pools, tenant-level KV cache, VPC peering) and what failure modes trigger tenant impact.
- Burst credits and throttles: defined burst windows, refill rates, and preemption policies for expansion beyond committed throughput.
- Fallbacks: compatibility of fallback models (e.g., quantized variants) and automatic routing policies that maintain SLAs.

Example procurement-ready clause language (engineering-friendly):
- "Provider guarantees committed throughput of X tokens/sec across a dedicated GPU pool. Throughput is measured on agreed prompt set (appendix A) and evaluated using the provider's benchmark harness. Provider will maintain p95 latency <= Y ms and p99 latency <= Z ms for prompt sizes up to N tokens when within committed throughput."
- "Provider will isolate customer traffic to dedicated GPU pools segmented at the hypervisor/process level; no noisy-neighbor interference from other tenants is allowed except during scheduled maintenance windows or agreed emergency fallbacks."

Operational knobs and negotiation levers (what committees should ask for):
- Measured SLOs and test harness: insist on attaching a minimal reproducible prompt set and the benchmarking script to the contract.
- Burst capacity terms: negotiate explicit burst windows (e.g., 30s bursts up to 2x committed throughput with defined cooldown).
- Warmup/priming guarantees: requests to pre-warm KV/prefix caches for scheduled traffic spikes and a metric for cache hit ratio during warmup.
- Regional failover: clear RTO/RPO and expected latency delta when failing over to a different region or model variant.
- Data plane access controls: keys, encryption-at-rest/ transit, and audit log retention windows.

Common seller-to-buyer messaging patterns (short scripts for AE/SE):
- For SRE/infra: "We ship dedicated pools with hypervisor-level isolation and per-customer KV cache partitions to remove noisy neighbor variance. Your p95 latency targets are guaranteed under the committed throughput — we attach the benchmark harness to the agreement so your team can validate."
- For procurement/finance: "We map committed throughput to predictable monthly cost and include burst credits so you don't pay for transient demand. Additional capacity is available as an overage or a short-term burst purchase."
- For legal/compliance: "Private control plane option with VPC peering, KMS integration, and audit logs retained for X days. We support SOC2/audit artifacts on request."
message_matrix:
Use-case quadrant -> Topline ask -> Technical proof point -> Negotiation fallback:
- Latency-sensitive real-time UI -> Low p99 latency, low jitter -> p99 measured on agreed prompt set; CDN-style prefix caching -> Fallback to smaller context models + local quantized variant
- High-throughput batch embeddings -> Committed tokens/sec, predictable hourly throughput -> sustained tokens/sec numbers + job scheduling windows -> Allow burst credits or scheduled reservations
- Regulated data / PII -> Data plane isolation and in-transit encryption -> VPC, dedicated disk/instance + KMS -> Add NDA/data processing addendum and extended audit logs

Example quick-rebuttals to competitive tropes:
- Competitor: "Shared multi-tenant is cheaper; dedicated isn't worth it." -> Rebuttal: "Cheaper up-front, but shared systems add variance and unpredictable tail latencies; for customer-facing SLAs that variance is equivalent to business risk and hidden cost. We can show modeled cost-of-not-meeting-SLA with sample traffic."
- Competitor: "We provide automatic scaling so committed capacity is unnecessary." -> Rebuttal: "Automatic scaling introduces cold-starts and potential throttling; for sustained high throughput and tight latency SLOs committed capacity ensures consistent node allocation and KV cache residency."
competitor_notes:
Short competitor mapping for technical PO/SE prep:
- Vendor A: emphasizes autoscaling and serverless endpoints; weak on isolation guarantees and burst semantics. Question to ask: how do you measure noisy-neighbor impact? Can we reserve pool slices?
- Vendor B: on-prem appliance; strong isolation but slow upgrade/rollout cadence and difficult cross-region redundancy. Question to ask: lead time for firmware/model upgrades and whether they provide fallback variants with minimal operator intervention.
- Vendor C: lower list price but shared pools and opaque kernel-level optimizations. Question: can they attach a benchmark harness and allow third-party testing?

Procurement-ready checklist (use at negotiation kickoff):
- [ ] Attach benchmark harness (repro script + prompt set) to SOW/appendix.
- [ ] Define committed throughput metric and measurement window (tokens/sec, p95 over 24h).
- [ ] Define latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99 for stated prompt sizes).
- [ ] Specify isolation model (dedicated GPU pool, KV cache partitioning, network controls).
- [ ] Define burst credit policy (size, refill, cost model).
- [ ] Regional failover RTO/RPO and expected latency delta.
- [ ] Security/compliance addenda: KMS integration, audit log retention, SOC2 artifacts.
- [ ] Incident escalation path and runbook handoff SLA.
- [ ] Pricing floors for committed capacity and overage pricing table.
- [ ] Scheduled maintenance windows and notification lead time.

Notes from SE rehearsal (phrasing to avoid):
- Avoid absolutes like "zero risk" or "perfect isolation"; prefer measurable language and defined exceptions.
- Don't bury fallback costs in a long appendix; surface them as a short table in the SOW.

Appendix ideas (to add to final SOW):
- Appendix A: canonical prompt set used for throughput/latency measurements.
- Appendix B: benchmark harness link + versioned docker image + baseline metrics.
- Appendix C: incident runbook for capacity-related outages and contact chain.
procurement_checklist:
See checklist in body section. Copyable items for SOW additions:
- Committed throughput: [numeric value] tokens/sec, measurement harness link: [url]
- Latency SLOs: p95 <= [ms], p99 <= [ms] for prompt sizes up to [N tokens]
- Isolation: dedicated GPU pool with per-tenant KV cache partitions and VPC peering option
- Burst credits: [x] minutes per month at up to [y]x commit, refill policy: [policy]
- Failover: RTO [hours], RPO [minutes], expected latency delta [ms]
- Audit logs: retention [days], exportable to buyer SIEM: yes/no
